An long short-term memory (LSTM) model is trained to account for time-variant channel dynamics and is integrated with a existing deep learning approach that utilizes spatial averaging to improve resolution. Simulation results indicate that the combined LSTM approach yields a higher success rate in deep learning-assisted channel estimation.

The goal of image tinting is to add a color map to a grayscale image, and typically, this is accomplished using a traditional image processing technique that relies on local color averages from a reference library image. Nonetheless, this approach is susceptible to noise and errors, particularly if the reference image is not accurately aligned. In contrast, a more recent method utilizes a Generative Adversarial Network to tackle this task, effectively incorporating global characteristics of a large dataset. Despite its advantages, this approach is computationally demanding and can produce artifacts. To address these limitations, we introduce an improved workflow that combines a generative network with an affine transformation, and aligns the input grayscale image with a reference color map through a stabilization step. Our approach outperforms traditional and recent methods in terms of accuracy and robustness, as demonstrated on the Celestial dataset. Moreover, we showcase our results on the wilds dataset, specifically on aerial images.

In the realm of supervised learning, a particular neural network architecture is capable of accurately mimicking complex functions despite being subject to arbitrary input and output constraints. This notable property is rooted in the Universal Approximation Theorem. We propose an innovative approach, dubbed UAT-NNS, that leverages this theorem to bypass the conventional need for optimizing network weights. Instead, UAT-NNS employs an optimal function to achieve near sample-perfect error performance, showcasing an unprecedented aspect of neural networks as feature-extraction machines. Since UAT-NNS avoids training in the classical sense, it is resistant to overfitting and exhibits enhanced generalization capabilities. We have formally established the robustness of UAT-NNS across a wide range of input data, even in the presence of noisy inputs. Experimental results, encompassing various benchmark problems and multiple error metrics, have substantiated our theoretical findings, highlighting UAT-NNS's superior performance compared to standard neural networks.

This article serves as an introduction to an informal series of reports detailing the accomplishments and experiences of ECFA Early Career Researcher committees. Formed in 2021 to support the needs of young researchers, these committees have successfully undertaken a range of tasks including surveys, focus groups, and task forces. Their endeavors have resulted in numerous recommendations on topics like work-life balance, mental health, and diversity and inclusion. Furthermore, several committees have established resources such as online communities, mentorship programs, and handbooks to sustain their efforts. The mentioned committees' activities are highlighted, with more to be covered in future reports.

Researchers built and studied an acoustic metastructure consisting of two interconnected arrays of tubes with resonating lengths in relation to sound frequencies. This metastructure was tested using sound waves of varying frequencies, and the experiments revealed that acoustic energy can be manipulated and directed between the two arrays. Notably, the concept and design of this metastructure are inspired by nanoscale metal structures known as dual-line gratings, which were found to influence light behavior in studies. Our studies have shown that acoustic systems can be designed with similar properties, opening up possibilities for developing new devices that control sound waves.

This paper introduces a revolutionary approach to machine learning that enables robots to adapt through hands-on experience. We've developed a versatile red-green-blue (RGB) system that effectively communicates high-level learning strategies to robots, demonstrating excellent performance across a wide range of tasks. The RGB framework has the added benefit of being platform-independent, allowing it to be applied to any type of robot without restriction. Furthermore, its modular structure makes it applicable to tasks involving multiple robots, as seen in our multi-agent learning scenario. We showcase the capabilities of our cognitive AI framework through a real-world demonstration of human-robot cooperative learning.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the average absolute deviation around the median. The average absolute deviation is a popular measure of variability. When the data follow a normal distribution, this measure is related to the standard deviation by the relationship $MAD/\sigma = 0.74 + 1.05/\sqrt{2n}$. Based on this relationship, a new family of bias-corrected estimators for the average absolute deviation has been formulated. The estimators work well in small samples, ranging from 3 to 100. The performance of these estimators is evaluated under various data generation mechanisms. The bias-corrected estimators are compared with alternative methods, including the mean absolute deviation and the interquartile range. The integration of these estimators into the R programming language is demonstrated, along with an example of their application to real data.

Unlabeled knowledge graphs present a significant challenge for link prediction tasks due to their vast number of possible connections. Current approaches rely heavily on the properties of entities, such as their labels or descriptions, to make predictions. However, these methods fall short in the context of unlabeled knowledge graphs. To overcome this issue, we've developed a new task called connection prediction, which involves identifying missing relationships between entities in the graph. We've established a bi-directional correspondence between our proposed task and relation discovery in unsupervised knowledge graph reasoning. Additionally, we've designed two cutting-edge models, $K$-$M$ $F$ and $M$ $F$ $_{w/o}$ $R$, to tackle connection prediction, which achieve remarkable results on existing datasets, and show promising results on a newly created dataset through the implementation of early stopping.

To study the breakdown of quarkonia in a non-zero momentum-aligned QCD environment with anisotropy, we develop a theoretical framework. We investigate the behavior of a complex quark and an antiquark in an anisotropic plasma using an approximate method that takes into account finite baryonic chemical potential and temperature. Our analysis is based on a specific model and we calculate the binding energy of quarkonia in n-dimensional space. We also consider finite baryonic chemical potential and temperature effects on the light and heavy quark states. We evaluate the characteristics of quarkonium disruption under the influence of anisotropy in n-dimensional, 3-dimensional, and 2-dimensional spaces. We analyze the impact of anisotropy on the light and heavy quark state stability. We compare our results with theoretical and experimental findings in anisotropic plasma with finite baryonic chemical potential and temperature.

We investigated the magnetic arrangements of Tb3RuO7 and Tb3OsO7 using neutron-diffraction experiments.
Tb3RuO7 exhibits alternating-bond chain behavior with incommensurate magnetic patterns, caused by an uneven internal magnetic field from neighboring terbium ions.
This unique situation leads to an intermediate disordered state due to competing interactions between incommensurate and commensurate ordering forces.
Conversely, Tb3OsO7 shows a uniformly aligned chain pattern with antiferromagnetic properties, osmium being aligned parallel to the crystal axis.

Deep learning models excel in creating detailed representations of data, but they often overlook important spatial relationships within the context of computer vision. To address this limitation, our research focuses on developing a novel feature extraction method that balances complexity and interpretability. Our modulated cyclic activation-cum-rotation-invariance technique is integrated into convolutional neural networks, enabling it to detect local features and their relative positions within images. Due to its effectiveness in capturing both low and high-level image details, our modulated cyclic activation-cum-rotation-invariance technique achieves remarkable performance in 13 benchmark datasets, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods significantly. Our findings are further enhanced by the insights gained into the features being learned within our modulated cyclic activation-cum-rotation-invariance technique.

Machine learning models learn from data uniformly sampled from a domain, yet they often fail in settings where the distribution of data changes over time (covariate shift). We've developed a novel semi-generative approach using influence functions to update existing models and address this issue. Our method relies on two types of information: cause attributes, which signal feature importance, and effect attributes, which represent model outputs. We've established a framework for semi-generative influence functions that can be applied in various settings, including kernel-based models and neural networks, while also proposing a new algorithm for gradient boosting models. Experimental results in synthetic and real-world settings demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

Despite its impressive performance in various tasks, the inner workings of deep learning models remain poorly understood. To address this lack of insight, we are exploring the geometric principles that govern deep learning models. By reimagining neural networks through a geometric lens, we can gain profound insights into their behavior. We use advanced differential geometry concepts, such as manifolds, connections, and curvatures, to model neural networks. This approach enables us to apply sophisticated mathematical techniques from quantum gravity and string theory to investigate the global properties of neural networks. We are leveraging the geometric structure of these models to develop new training methods and evaluation metrics, and we are applying advanced mathematical operators to enhance the models' performance. We are also incorporating concepts from group theory and representation theory into our framework, allowing for the comparison and transfer of knowledge across different neural network architectures. With this powerful mathematical toolkit, we are working to uncover the underlying universal laws that govern deep learning models, ultimately facilitating the development of self-improving systems that we terms 'intellectual animals.'

A prime ideal in a polynomial ring contains a unique non-constant polynomial, known as a chief ideal, that is maximally divisible by that prime ideal. Similarly, in the division ring of fractions of an integral domain, an ideal contains a unique non-zero element, referred to as a chief element, that is maximally divisible by that ideal. This research involves proving that certain properties of this chief element correspond to properties of the lattice depth of the ideal in question. Additionally, the study relates these properties to properties of prime ideals within a polynomial ring.

Machine learning techniques have gained significant attention in recent years, particularly in medical research, where they are used to analyze complex medical images and identify suitable treatments based on a patient's characteristics. However, there is a lack of transparent decision-making processes in these models, which raises concerns in high-stakes medical decisions. To address this issue, we have developed a framework that enables explanation through feature importance, showcasing that the incorporation of specialist variables can significantly enhance model performance. Our results indicate that incorporating these variables elevates the accuracy of jet classifiers from 45% to 75%. Furthermore, our approach successfully transmitted layer-wise relevance to the final classification decision, demonstrating that the incorporation of specialist variables is a necessary component for accurate classification.

For any positive integers r and n, we define a Stirling number of the second kind as ${n\choose r}$, and explore a variation of it, denoted by ${n_r}^{(k)}$, which counts the ways to partition a set of n items into k non-empty subsets, where each subset has at least r items. We establish a differential equation to represent this modified Stirling number and use it to prove a closure property. We show that a polynomial sequence solves this equation if and only if it satisfies a specific recursion formula, leading to a classification of such sequences. We further find a universal generating function for the ${n_r}^{(k)}$ numbers, providing additional insight and understanding into this generalization of Stirling numbers.

One-dimensional non-crystallographic lattices are categorized into 32 groups, 17 of which have local symmetry. Among these, the five families represented by ash layers exhibit a unique characteristic. By reducing these layers to one-dimensional lattices, the ash groups can be mapped to a new set of 10 groups. Additionally, the doubling of these lattices leads to the formation of 32 groups, known as sn layers. Analyzing the automorphisms within the local symmetry of ash layers reveals the creation of an extensive set of two-dimensional groups, consisting of 18 families, each with diverse properties and complexities.

Momentum operators are explored in the context of a curved spacetime. It is demonstrated that an operator defining a momentum vector can be expressed as the derivative of a function along a geodesic line with respect to proper time, where the function represents the advanced distance along that geodesic. The choice of a specific geodesic is linked to a choice of Killing vector field, which is discussed in more detail. The article then discusses the properties of commutators of these momentum operators, particularly in relation to the layout of a spacetime. The implications of these findings for second quantization are also considered.

Artificial neural networks have significant potential in tackling complex problems from the fields of quantum chemistry and condensed matter physics. However, their application to many-body systems like the Hubbard model is hindered by the inherent ambiguities present in the wavefunction phase. We introduce a new type of neural network that avoids this issue, using complex-valued weights and propagators instead of the traditional real-valued approach. Results show that this approach is capable of accurately determining the ground state energy within 1% error, something that has been a long-standing challenge.

A possible connection exists between the Standard Model's (SM) flavor sector and the origin of the Higgs boson. Within composite higgs models featuring an approximate $SO(5)$ global symmetry, the flavor sector and Higgs sector are integrated. Here, the flavor sector is described by a set of vector-like irredutible representations, leading to an effective lagrangian that includes a variety of operators. These assumptions result in a diverse set of flavon-Higgs interactions. By attributing the flavor hierarchy to a set of flavon non-linear sigma model fields, an effective lagrangian is formulated, incorporating both flavon and Higgs fields. By applying an $SO(5) \to SO(4) \times SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_R$ symmetry breaking, a bottom-up approach is adopted to investigate various aspects of the framework. Case studies are provided to illustrate the type of predictions that can emerge in this framework, concerning phenomena like rare $K$ decays, the Hill-Samuelson parameter, and particle lightest Higgs boson observables.

User-immersive virtual reality experiences are characterized by perceptual transformations of visual and auditory information, distorting awareness of physical reality. These transformations create a VR'shadow zone', hiding users' awareness of real-world circumstances, while simultaneously revealing their compromised judgment in that environment. We introduce the concept of the shadow zone, exploring its psychological and philosophical implications, and investigating how Compromised Judgment Thresholds are affected through a user study. Our research reveals that these thresholds can be predicted by the level of distortion introduced in VR, as validated through statistical analysis. Our study provides insight into the psychological limitations of VR users, with potential consequences on design practices, including the consideration of 'user presence' in VR applications.

Currently, modern machine translation systems excel in well-resourced languages, but performance suffers significantly in areas like North African Arabic and Basque. A major obstacle is the scarcity of high-quality training data available for these languages. The emergence of large-scale pre-trained multilingual models offers hope, but their effectiveness in low-resourced settings remains untested. In this research, we build upon these models by adapting them to integrate with modern transformer-based architectures, then subject them to extensive training with limited data for languages under-resourced. Our results show improvements over traditional approaches, highlighting the potential for these models to address language resource gaps. Encouraged by these findings, we've open-sourced our implementation, aiming to stimulate innovation in low-resourced language settings.

Using advanced computational models, a critical phenomenon is identified in which a system composed of orbiting matter splits into multiple components under the influence of gravitational forces. This process is triggered when angular momentum exceeds a specific threshold and mass is evenly distributed. As the parent core's mass increases, the likelihood of system disintegration rises and can reach 90% in certain scenarios, with the mass range impacted expanding by approximately three orders of magnitude. It is discovered that the mass of components formed during this process aligns closely with a particular mass range and varies little in response to changes in the core's mass. Furthermore, it is found that the number of components created can range from two to eleven, with each configuration possessing its own total and system mass.

M-ar-K-Fast Autoencoders are a type of linear regression-based, efficient method for solving dimensionality reduction problems. They utilize a matrix representation of the data and a non-negative decomposition of the encoded features to facilitate learning, thereby eliminating the need for complex neural networks. We develop an unsupervised two-stage approach for training M-ar-K-Fast Autoencoders, with theoretical support from the frame representation property. Our method allows for the optimization of frame parameters, enabling control over encoding features and subsequent reconstruction of the original data. We evaluate our model on diverse datasets, achieving superior results for feature extraction and representation with reduced computational complexity.

This paper revisits the link between finite model theory and algebraic methods for logic and cryptography by examining several complexity bounds for logic formulas that rely on specific types of algebraic computations. The specific thresholds evaluated are: log n (for small constants), log^2n, n^2/4, n/2, n, and 2^n. Each of these thresholds is connected to distinct properties of diagrams, particularly in choiceless polynomial time with duration, and is also related to various extensions of the polynomial calculus. The key findings demonstrate the tightness of log n and n/2 bounds, whereas the other bounds are shown to be less accurate and may be surpassed by specific strategies. The results are further illustrated by an approach to identify if a structure contains the properties of a specific finite model, utilizing a particular DPTD diagram.

We introduce an infinite sequence of $\sigma$-elementary rings, thereby establishing a new category of $\sigma$-unital algebras beyond the C*-algebras. Our construction also yields a vast number of non-isomorphic $\sigma$-unital algebras. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of the lower semi-continuous derivation on the collection of reduced $\sigma$-unital algebras is provided.

Unverifiable assumptions and framework-based meta-theories are indispensable tools for establishing the correctness of software and hardware systems. Unlike traditional soundness theorems, these frameworks lack a clear definition, which has led to differing interpretations and implementations. Researchers face challenges in comparing various frameworks due to a lack of consensus on their definition. This issue is particularly evident in the program logic community, where designers of program logics often rely on unverifiable assumptions and leverage the framework to ensure the correct implementation of their design. To address this problem, we introduce a novel approach that explores the concept of a framework by identifying its essential components and evaluating its applicability to established program logics, including SAW, MLV, and BoR. By doing so, we contribute to the development of a clear and concise definition for program logics, thereby facilitating comparisons and assessments of their design.

The proliferation of social media has generated vast amounts of location-specific data, providing unprecedented insight into real-time spatial dynamics and crowd behavior. This research tackles the challenge of identifying and categorizing concurrent events within a specified area, utilizing Bayesian models to filter out false positives from the data streams. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying it to Twitter feeds, leveraging the API's capacity limit to collect relevant data sets. The output of our system is a dynamic visualization depicting the temporal sequence and spatial distribution of detected events, alongside the number of users involved.

The CMB lensing convergence bias and variance can be estimated by analyzing the distortion of angular bispectrum in a small, non-linear area around a specified point, and this method has shown accurate results through simulations. It's a quickly calculable technique that doesn't require significant analysis and can be used with existing data, and it could be useful for testing new lensing parameters without needing additional data.

To ensure reliable Bayesian estimation, including parameter estimation and prediction, in the presence of an adversary, we develop a robust framework. Adversarial resistance is achieved by incorporating certification bounds into the posterior distribution. These bounds are generated using a certified trust region method adapted from adversarial training techniques in deep learning. A straightforward adaptation of standard Bayesian methods using non-certified methods is insufficient, as they would fail to meet the required standards. Instead, we show that Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithms utilizing certified proposals meet the requirements, allowing for efficient computation. Specifically, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in Gaussian and mixed-effect Gaussian models under various types of adversaries.

Digital rumors spreading through social media platforms have caused significant issues worldwide, while China's tightly controlled internet environment initially led researchers to believe it was a low-risk region. However, the sudden outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic in China created an ideal environment for digital rumors to flourish. This research reveals that in the early stages of the pandemic, multiple digital rumors regarding the outbreak were disseminated rapidly across Chinese social media platforms before eventually being counteracted by official disinformation campaigns. We examine the characteristics of users who engage in digital rumor dissemination, including their online behavior and how these rumors spread across different online communities. Our findings show that digital rumors often targeted specific groups, and users who promoted them tended to have been previously active in online discussions. Additionally, users who had been punished in the past for similar behavior were less likely to participate in digital rumor dissemination. This research provides insights that can help in designing more effective countermeasures to stop the spread of digital rumors, while also highlighting the challenges in completely eliminating all digital rumors in environments with limited online transparency and trust.

This research investigates the effect of dimensionality reduction on hyperspectral image analysis. Spectral dimensionality reduction techniques minimize data complexity while maintaining relevant features for further processing. The study focuses on the Hyperspectral Pixel Categorization task, where the goal is to identify features that best represent each class with minimal relevance to the spatial arrangement of pixels. We compared the performance of five widely used techniques - Principal Component Analysis, Independent Component Analysis, Fast Independent Component Analysis, Minimum Volume Buffering, and Fast Minimum Volume Buffering - on a real-world dataset, examining their outcomes through various perspectives, including numerical quantification, visual evaluation, and statistical analysis. The results show that FICA and FMB outperformed other methods, improving the accuracy of classification models and reducing data complexity, while their fast versions exhibited comparable performance to their slower counterparts. The study's findings highlight the importance of considering the computational trade-offs of these methods in real-world applications.

There is no universally acceptable definition for natural language, which has led to a diverse range of formal frameworks and interpretations. Despite their numerous variations, many of these frameworks share key similarities and can be viewed as specific realizations of a broader, more fundamental concept. In this study, we identify common aspects of natural language frameworks by reducing them to a unified type of mathematical structure, which we call a 'protoschema'. A protoschema serves as a schema that various language models can instantiate. We demonstrate the applicability of our approach by incorporating six prominent language frameworks, thereby offering new insights into them from an algebraic and categorical perspective.

A newly developed tool called ProVerde takes into account the diversity of amide proton chemical shifts in proteins by integrating machine learning algorithms and quantum mechanics, thereby refining the protein structure. ProVerde's learning model is based on 37 million calculated amide proton chemical shift values, which were determined using advanced computational methods based on quantum physics. The tool was tested using 221 proteins in the Protein Data Bank and showed positive results in evaluating the quality of protein models. A version of the tool specifically designed for molecular dynamics simulations is also available, which can provide ongoing analysis and feedback during simulation runs. The tool has been determined to be accurate and reliable and is now available for public use.

In recent years, the choice of loss function in deep learning models has received more attention. This study examines the impact of modifying loss functions during training. To achieve this, we conducted a comprehensive investigation involving 13, 42, and 59 classification datasets from various domains. The experiment compared the effectiveness of seven different loss functions when combined with three commonly applied regularization methods. The analysis reveals that altering the loss function typically reduces the model's accuracy, though this decline is less pronounced with categorical cross-entropy. A statistical assessment of the results indicates that cross-entropy with exponential loss is a reliable and efficient choice, outperforming other combinations in our investigation.

Describing the behaviors of complex systems comprised of strongly interacting elements requires concise expressions for their internal relationships. By breaking down a comprehensive interaction into four distinct components, researchers can develop a theoretical framework to model these interactions numerically. From a mathematical perspective, this approach can be formalized using a specific type of diagrammatic expansion, which we reexamine through the lens of perturbation theory. By correlating the four-component interactions with basic four-particle processes, we can establish a set of Hamiltonian-based models that accurately represent these interactions. Consequently, this methodology enables a comprehensive benchmarking of parquet theory's applicability to distinct physical systems.

We have developed a computationally efficient method to model the emergence of exciton condensation through the combination of light and matter interactions. This approach utilizes a hybrid framework, integrating ab initio density functional theory and the multiple scissors approximation, to resolve long-standing challenges associated with exciton condensation. Notably, our methodology enables the accurate determination of self-energy and effective masses without relying on perturbative methods. We have successfully applied this method to investigate exciton condensation in 2H-TiSe2 under pressure, yielding a detailed understanding of its electronic and phononic properties. Our results, obtained through ab initio density functional theory with the local density approximation, demonstrate significant agreement with existing experimental and theoretical data. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that electron-phonon interactions play a crucial role in promoting exciton condensation through the displacement of ions. Our methodology has the potential to contribute significantly to the study of exciton condensation and related phenomena in solids.

The effectiveness of community policing depends on various factors, including the quality of interactions between community members and law enforcement officials. To optimize these interactions, it is crucial to analyze the conversations, gather insights, and make data-driven decisions. However, current systems fail to capture the nuances of these conversations, primarily because they rely on infrequent in-person meetings between community members and dispatchers. To address this limitation, we developed a system that compensates for undercovered interactions by employing automatic text-based reporting tools. By leveraging this system, we were able to collect a substantial dataset of conversations, which we analyzed to extract valuable insights and facilitate data analysis for meaningful change.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on a nematic superconductor containing only triplet Cooper pairs, we employ a minimal Landau gauge theory. The model's response to a perpendicular magnetic field is characterized by two distinct curvature parameters related to its symmetry properties. The presence of Cooper pairs leads to two possible curvature parameters, which are both eliminated under the application of a strong magnetic field, resulting in paramagnetic properties. Our findings also reveal that the response of the nematic superconductor to an in-plane magnetic field is anisotropic, with its susceptibility varying based on the orientation of the Cooper pairs' momentum relative to the field. Our analysis provides a means to theoretically determine the direction of the Cooper pairs' momentum via magnetometry experiments.

Achieving curriculum objectives relies heavily on the combination of teaching methods that cater to different learning styles and levels of prior knowledge. A novel approach involves employing a minimax strategy, where the worst-case educational outcome is minimized. A mathematical framework supports the implementation of this approach, enabling a systematic teaching method to be derived. We demonstrate this concept through a simplified example, where a teacher seeks to educate students about various mathematical axioms, while a mischievous student strives to undermine their understanding. Furthermore, the example highlights a fundamental dilemma: incorporating diverse teaching methods proves beneficial, but only if one can anticipate the level of opposition.

Between 1750 and 1940, music notation became increasingly detailed, reflecting
increasing data complexity.  Researchers from Harvard and University College London
analysed music from the Bach Chorales, Mozart, Chopin, Debussy, Beethoven, and
Schubert to establish a comprehensive dataset, then employed sophisticated machine
learning techniques to define complexity measures.  They discovered that complexity
peaked during the Romantic era and found correlations between these measures.  In
a subsequent study, they investigated how modern music compares by analysing sound
recordings from Billboard charts between 1956 and 2006.  This work reveals that
modern music is both more complex and unpredictable than expected, with some
artists pushing boundaries of complexity.

We're examining a complex decision-making scenario where multiple options are available simultaneously. Each time a choice is made, the corresponding option receives a reward, and our goal is to identify which strategies yield the highest long-term rewards. A newly developed method is being tested for its ability to detect the top-performing strategies by analyzing the sequence of choices and rewards collected over time. Our investigation focuses on the most favored strategies using both the Birkhoff-von Neumann polytope and the Lebesgue measure on the polytope. As our analysis shows, the most preferred strategies converge at an exponential rate as the sequence of choices approaches a stationary distribution. This convergence rate exceeds what could be achieved using the Strong Law of Large Numbers alone. Additionally, our findings are supported by a companion test that identifies the top strategies simultaneously. Our investigation builds on prior research in Silvestrini, and extends it to multiple-choice scenarios, where the available strategies are unrestricted.

This study explores the concept of playfulness in a computational context through user interactions with and mental processes related to bugs in programs, highlighting the importance of playfulness through empirical observations and definitions from relevant fields. To establish a reliable measurement of playfulness in computational contexts, we analyzed reviews of games to identify common themes and developed the Playfulness in Code (PIC) framework. This framework, comprising three aspects of playfulness – novelty, structure, and ambiguity – is utilized to evaluate the level of playfulness within software projects. By applying the PIC framework, we analyzed various projects, including those focused on computational playfulness, such as bugs in programs, to determine how playfulness is perceived and implemented across different disciplines. Our analysis indicated that projects prioritizing playfulness often exhibit a higher level of novelty and clear structure, while those from disciplines emphasizing learning and education tend to incorporate ambiguous elements more frequently. Our findings also showed a positive correlation between the level of playfulness in software projects and their popularity, highlighted by projects exhibiting a higher level of playfulness experiencing greater growth in popularity.

In the realm of Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs), setting up optimal detection thresholds can be a daunting task, requiring substantial expertise and time. The process is further complicated by the necessity of balancing type I and type II errors. Since high-quality labeled datasets are difficult and time-consuming to obtain, researchers often employ reward learning approaches to aid in threshold setting. However, existing methods involve time-consuming data evaluation, typically involving visual analysis to determine the outcome of each data instance. To accelerate this process, we introduce a time-effective approach called Visually Supported Cluster Ranking (VSCR). VSCR group relevant data into clusters based on their features and assigns a reward to each based on a set of predefined evaluation criteria. Each instance within each cluster is then given the average reward as its outcome, reducing the time required for outcome determination. The VSCR approach enables more efficient processing of IDSs, allowing for quicker and more accurate tuning of detection thresholds.

We show that core-conciseness is a hereditary property in Smyth powerspaces, and thus, for any core-concise Smyth powerspace $X$, the collection of core-concise subsets of $X$ forms a Smyth powerspace. Moreover, we have characterized core-conciseness in Smyth powerspaces by means of upwelling sequences and stated conditions under which an orderly topological space is core-concise.

We've observed aimed vortex loops emerge in two-dimensional liquid simulations under specific conditions. When an external disturbance is introduced at a distance from the loop's center, it causes a tiny inner ring to rotate in the opposite direction. As the external disturbance is introduced closer to the center, it triggers the formation of a vortex loop through a process known as a vortex nucleation event. If the external disturbance is positioned within this 'vortex nucleation radius', the inner ring's rotation not only changes direction but also accelerates, leading to a significant increase in angular velocity once it crosses a certain threshold velocity. This sudden velocity surge is due to the conversion of the external disturbance's energy into kinetic energy as the vortex loop forms. We've identified another critical factor influencing aimed vortex loops: the relationship between the external disturbance's size and the area being measured. Aimed vortex loops only occur within a specific 'aimed velocity regime' defined by a minimum and maximum velocity range. Within this 'aimed velocity regime', the area being measured appears to be reduced in size, indicating that aimed vortex loops are indeed characterized by a minimized or eliminated area being measured. We've identified two critical factors influencing aimed velocity loops: the distance between the external disturbance and the loop's center and the external disturbance's size. We've calculated and provided the mathematical expressions for both of these factors. We've also determined that the 'aimed velocity regime' not only depends on the distance between the external disturbance and the loop's center but also

To improve short-term forecasting, a new method combines an enhanced form of inverse likelihood weighting with future predictions from models like ARIMA and neural networks. This technique addresses issues with temporal dependence and informed forecasting, making it more resilient to predictions of upcoming trends. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by showcasing its superior performance on real-world data, specifically life expectancy in the US from 1860 to 1869 as analyzed in Table 1.

Our analysis suggests that the theoretical description of hadronic interactions is inadequate, particularly at low energy levels. By cross-referencing data from the Frascati rho meson decay experiment with theoretical predictions from the Chiral Perturbation Theory, we've discovered a significant discrepancy of approximately 4 standard deviations. This finding highlights the necessity for a novel theoretical framework incorporating the tau lepton mass, a requirement set forth by Accuracy Tau Physics.

A fundamental problem in fluid dynamics, baroclinic wave development in a spinning annulus, has been extensively studied through both computational and experimental approaches. Despite previous research, there are ongoing debates regarding the dynamics of these waves and how they interact with the vortex stretching process and wave instability. To contribute to this field, a new dataset has been collected through a collaborative effort between researchers using both computational and experimental methods. The findings from these studies have been compared and integrated in a comprehensive report. The observed results include the impact of wave instability, wave-slip friction, and vortex intensity on the dynamics. The comparison between experimental and computational results has been presented in detail, along with a discussion on the discrepancies and similarities between the two approaches. The collected results are available in an open-access platform for further research references.

We introduce a convenient transformation of Bayesian estimation models for extreme values that involves a simpler point process reparametrization. The new parameterization makes it easier to sample from the posterior distribution, especially when working with gradient-based methods. This reformulation also enables a more efficient exploration of the model space, as it reduces the correlation between sampling iterations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this parameterization through simulations and the analysis of real data from rainfall observations in the United Kingdom.

In the context of offline reinforcement learning, our research focuses on how to optimize decision-making policies when a portion of the available data is inaccurate. This problem is examined from two perspectives: determining the least amount of corrupt data that can be tolerated and finding the best policy despite some level of corrupt data. Analyzing the interplay between the amount of corrupt data and its impact on offline RL policy optimization yields important insights. Moreover, our work introduces two new metrics to evaluate the robustness of offline RL policies and presents two methodological contributions: an approach to identify the maximum amount of corrupt data tolerated and a data-efficient method to find the best policy despite some level of corrupt data. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed methods in real-world scenarios.

This study uses the Obuchi-Takada method to introduce a new concept of strong positivity for positive solutions of parabolic equations. This approach is applied to a solution's sign pattern, and we investigate the manageability of certain nonlinear boundary value problems related to the 1-D heat equation.

Understanding and mitigating the adverse effects of out-of-distribution (OOD) behavior in machine learning models is a critical research area. In the context of text-based models, specifically in the areas of text classification and text generation, identifying and quantifying OOD categories is a key challenge. Current studies lack a unified understanding of OOD categories and do not provide comprehensive evaluation metrics. To address this gap, we develop a framework for OOD categories in text-based scenarios and establish a dataset with annotated category labels, as well as proposed evaluation metrics. Our work is grounded in the concept of discordance, which measures the divergence of a model's output distribution from its training counterpart. The resulting evaluation metrics encompass two types: those that assess an model's conformity by comparing its performance within and outside its defined scope, and those that examine a model's behavior across various distribution changes. Our study includes a thorough evaluation of these metrics using our constructed dataset with human annotations.

This research outlines a theoretical model describing Brownian molecular machines powered by inelastic electron tunneling. The proposed mechanism involves two nanoscale components: donor and acceptor molecules. The donor molecule acts as an energetic fountain, emitting photons when in an excited state. The acceptance molecule has a ground state energy level aligned with the donor's emission spectrum, enabling it to absorb photons and transition into a higher energy state. The system's excited state properties are analyzed through a series of simulations, resulting in the identification of a stationary point representing the system's equilibrium state. The stationary point confirms the existence of a thermodynamic cycle, facilitating the investigation of efficiency and efficiency maximization under isolated conditions. The theoretical framework presented here provides a foundational understanding of Brownian molecular machines and may be applied to various systems with modified parameters to align them with experimental setups.

We define a versatile concept - unidirectional resynchronizability - which extends existing notions of synchronizability and applies broadly across different types of automata, including word transducers, and we examine its fundamental properties. Notably, any unidirectional resynchronizability related to a right-linear identity-free word transducer can be expressed through a single input direction, and this insight leads to a straightforward algorithm for determining if such a property exists. Moreover, we find that for any word transducer, its left and right unidirectional resynchronizability are equivalently related to its respective left and right linear closure.

In various fields like number theory, combinatorics, and computer science, generalizing the concept of convolution has been a key area of study. This paper presents an efficient algorithm for computing a specific type of generalized convolution more quickly than the standard brute-force approach. The proposed method exploits previously overlooked properties of the underlying polynomial rings and their multiplication. By optimizing this calculation, the new algorithm can take advantage of existing factorization techniques to reduce its computational load.

The discovery of GJ 229B, the initial T-dwarf companion, was notable not only for being the first such finding but also because it offered insight into planet formation processes, given that its host star is relatively young. As a result, this system serves as a natural laboratory for investigating the evolution of planetary systems. To optimize the utilization of future spectrographs, such as the JWST, our research aims to examine the properties of GJ 229B and its environment through data analysis using the APOLLO code. APOLLO is a cutting-edge tool that excels in accurately determining atmospheric and physical properties of extra-solar planets and brown dwarfs by employing a Bayesian approach in conjunction with diverse observational constraints. By applying this code to GJ 229B, our team obtained precise estimates of the object's mass, size, atmospheric composition, and orbital characteristics. These findings position GJ 229B as a system that deviates from typical predictions made by planetary formation theories, indicating evaporating or scattered planets that require further examination.

To describe the behavior of a system with a low-energy region that varies slowly with angle, we need to go beyond the conventional description. Initially, researchers found that a $J^{--}$ state with $P=+1$ could be responsible, but subsequent calculations showed that loops involving quarks dominate the low-energy area, indicating a potential issue. Further investigation into the properties of the system is needed to determine if a $P=-1$ state or another phenomenon is responsible for the observed slow-angle variation.

We have calculated the decay width variations for several CP-violating processes involving charm and bottom mesons, specifically $\Kp\to\Kp\gamma\gamma$, $\Kp\to\Ks\gamma\gamma$, and $\Bd\to\Js\gamma\gamma$, which are influenced by the $\phi_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ parameters. Utilizing theoretical predictions and experimental data from LHCb, we have extracted new upper limits on these parameters: $\phi_s < 0.0836$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s < 0.0936$, both with 95% confidence. These results were obtained by combining the three decays in a single analysis. Additionally, we have calculated the $\phi_s$ values for individual decays, finding $\phi_s(-\Dz\to\Kp\Km) < 0.0934$, $\phi_s(\Bs\to\Ks\J/\psi) < 0.0908$, and $\phi_s(\Bd\to\Js\gamma\gamma) < 0.0905$, each with 95% confidence.

Understanding and predicting the spread of infectious diseases within a closed environment, such as a bus, requires considering both individual behavior and air circulation dynamics. This study, however, reveals that individual behavior plays a significantly greater role in the spread of infectious diseases, compared to air circulation. Our research integrates epidemiological modeling with a framework for estimating the effects of exposure, using data from an urban bus ride. We analyzed data from a 105-minute bus journey, collecting information on passenger movement, as well as respiratory and speech-generated virus emissions and transmission. Our analysis found that a highly infectious individual can cause transmissions in up to 30% of passengers, and that aggressive hygiene practices could potentially eliminate transmissions in up to 70% of cases.

The $\beta$ decay properties of $^{135,137}$Te isotopes were studied using the shell-model with the PD-MSDI interaction. The calculated half-lives and atomic mass excess values for $^{135}$Te and $^{137}$Te decayed into $^{135}$I and $^{137}$I, respectively, were found to align closely with experimental data. The results from theoretical calculations were then compared with experimental $\log ft$ values for various transitions. The comparisons revealed substantial agreement between calculated and experimental $\log ft$ values for both isotopes, with discrepancies being relatively minor. The good alignment of results was attributed to the effectiveness of the PD-MSDI interaction in describing the shell-model characteristics of these Te isotopes.

A recent double-faced auction protocol has been modified to accommodate transactions in virtual marketplaces. This modified auction, termed as Double Faced Auction with Authenticity (DFA), incorporates digital signatures to mitigate cheating in a decentralized system. Specifically, DFA has been enhanced with a faulty detection mechanism in two ways: firstly by utilizing a signature count-based approach; secondly by employing a one-way hash function combined with a public key. Furthermore, an experiment was conducted to evaluate the efficacy of DFA on a decentralized marketplace, utilizing Ethereum as the underlying network. This study demonstrates that DFA successfully prevents cheating and detects fraudulent activities in a reliable manner.

In a bottom-up meson composed of a bottom quark and a light quark (either up, down, or charm), the light quark is assumed to be at the ground state.  The mass of the meson can be calculated using a heavy quark effective theory (HQET) framework, which considers the bottom quark as heavy.  The calculation incorporates three components: the bottom quark mass, a light quark propagator, and a weak interaction represented by a gluon.  The gluon's contribution is considered to be negligible in a short-range distance context.  The mass of the meson is determined as the sum of the bottom quark mass and the light quark mass.  Specifically, examininations of four F-wave bottom mesons (denoted as $f_0(500)$, $\kappa(800)$, $F_1(1420)$, and $F'(1)(425)$ are conducted, which consider a light quark having zero orbital angular momentum due to the ground state requirement.  As a result, these examinations are considered not applicable, which leads to the conclusion that the approach is not suitable for calculating masses of particles with complex quark configurations.

A composition of real functions on an interval is a mapping from one interval to another that can be represented as the result of the union of translated functions, where translation occurs over the real line. We define a periodic composition as a composition whose component functions exhibit periodic characteristics. Our investigation focuses on the properties of periodic compositions of nonexpansive functions, where a function is considered nonexpansive if the distance between its outputs corresponds to the distance between its inputs. Specifically, we determine the criteria under which a periodic composition of nonexpansive functions yields a monotone curve when analyzed in the plane.

In various fields of data-driven dynamics research, dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) has emerged as a crucial tool. However, the standard DMD algorithm may produce inaccurate results when working with noisy data, a common problem in real-world applications. To address this limitation, the LANDO algorithm has been developed as an optimized kernel DMD (KD) implementation. Unlike other KD-based methods that focus on enhancing DMD's capabilities, LANDO is specifically designed to enhance DMD's accuracy and robustness. By incorporating a clarification optimization step and utilizing a kernel-based approach, LANDO is capable of processing high-dimensional nonlinear data while producing results that align with physical laws and are resistant to noise. To achieve this, LANDO incorporates a co-regularization method that integrates multiple models formed by different kernel embeddings. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the authors of this paper have successfully applied LANDO to simulate a Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard flow and a chaotic Lorenz system, showcasing its ability to produce accurate results from noisy data.

The objective of this study is to examine chess openings by leveraging data from the online chess community, specifically by analyzing posts from the largest chess forum, discussing strategies and ideas. A novel approach to categorizing openings is presented, which focuses on the connections between different chess strategies rather than traditional static classifications. This approach measures the complexity of each opening by identifying sub-groups within it and assessing the coherence of statements about the opening. Furthermore, the study uses social network metrics to evaluate the relationships between different openings, suggesting a theoretical framework for understanding chess openings.

This research explores the potential of accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs as a source of millisecond pulsars. We simulated 1.0 solar mass main-sequence stars within the 5-8 solar mass range evolving into main sequence, then onto the giant branch, and finally exploded as Type II supernovae, producing 1.3 solar mass neutron stars. Afterwards, these neutron stars underwent thermal evolution on the cooling curve. Various accretion rates were applied to simulate accretion from a binary companion, ultimately leading to a collapse of 50% of the neutron stars into black holes and 30% of the remaining neutron stars experiencing a pulsar explosion. Our findings on neutron star evolution align with existing studies, while those undergoing accretion show distinct thermal evolution patterns compared to non-accreted neutron stars. Pulsar properties, such as magnetic field strength and radius, are determined using the magnetized neutron star equation of state. Our study suggests that neutron stars experiencing accretion within a specific mass and radius range before collapse will have a radius greater than 12 km. This is in line with the observed characteristics of pulsars, where none have a radius below approximately 12 km. Our research indicates that the pulsar mass range is primarily determined by the binary companion mass, with a maximum mass range of approximately 0.05-0.4 solar masses. Lastly, our study implies that neutron star direct collapse into black holes is more likely than pulsar

A general approach to studying dynamical systems of any dimension is developed, 
utilizing a novel Lagrangian framework that incorporates both local and nonlocal components. 
The paper introduces a new set of variables, derived from the action principle, 
which serve as conservation laws. 
These variables are expressed in terms of the action function, 
and their existence is guaranteed regardless of the system's linearity or non-linearity. 
Furthermore, a new set of first integrals is identified, 
along with a corresponding set of Poisson commuting variables. 
Finally, the paper examines several well-known models, 
reconfirming previously established results in favor of the theory's validity.

Research in 3D object retrieval has primarily utilized 3D point cloud or mesh data,
encouraging retrieval approaches reminiscent of 2D image similarity search.
However, this method has limitations when users without 3D design knowledge attempt
to search for specific objects. To address this issue, we propose introducing a new
interface: a virtual reality (VR) drawing interface that allows users to create 2D
sketches in a 3-dimensional space using their hands or a stylus pen. These sketches
can be used to refine 3D shape queries, improving retrieval accuracy and efficiency.
Our study introduces a novel benchmark, called SD3, comprising of sketch-based 3D
object retrieval tasks. Additionally, we have designed and implemented VR tools to
enable test users to create their own database of 3D models with accompanying 2D
sketches based on an existing dataset called TOSCA. Our research provides a comprehensive
evaluation of state-of-the-art techniques on this new benchmark, aiming to stimulate
further advancements in the field.

The highly elliptical planet HD 80606 b, orbiting a solar-mass star in the constellation of Volans, presents a unique opportunity for scientists to utilize transit observations during its close approaches to Earth. With a highly irregular orbit, this planet offers a distinctive position in the sky around mid-April and November, corresponding to its planet transits, which can be used for precise scheduling through the consideration of its highly eccentric path. Observations collected during its 2009, 2010, 2011, 2013, 2015, 2017, 2019 transits were re-evaluated to refine the planet's movement and improve future prediction accuracy. Utilizing a mixture of data from telescope observations, both professional and amateur, the researchers have established an ephemeris model that accounts for the planet's movement with an error margin of 0.0006 days when considering all past observations and 0.0007 days when limiting the analysis to professional data alone. Based on this refined model, the predicted transit dates for HD 80606 b during the next decade were provided, showing that the planet's highly elliptical path aligns with a close approach to Earth on April 27, 2023, at 06:50 UTC, corresponding to a 0.065 magnitude dimming, which can be utilized by telescope observers worldwide to further collect data and revise the planet's movement.

In an ideal fluid with an isentropic collapse and a linear condition for pressure, there's a key connection between the fluid's density ($\rho$), pressure ($p$), and velocity potential ($f$), expressed as $p = \frac{C^2 \rho}{1 - \frac{\sigma}{2} \rho}$, where $C$ denotes sound speed and $\sigma$ denotes specific heat. This results in a second-order ordinary differential equation for the velocity potential, which has explicit solutions that apply globally in space and time. These solutions represent two-stage flows - spherically symmetric collapse and asymptotic tranquilization - and two-stage flows - planar collapse and asymptotic tranquilization. Additionally, there are two types of initial data sets that lead to divergent solutions: those that result in expanding fluids and those that result in contracting fluids. It's worth noting that when $\sigma > 2$, there are no feasible solutions; however, the mathematical feasibility of the solution does not assess the physical validity of the model. This model is compared to the polytropic gamma-gas model, which has more realistic behavior in some respects but lacks the simplicity of the linear model.

Extremal black holes exhibit unique characteristics due to their boundary between event horizons and causal boundaries. Research has been ongoing to understand the structure of these event horizons, with recent findings shedding new light on extremal black holes. Building upon previous work, particularly Iyer-Wald calculations, these amendments offer fresh insights into extremal black hole extremality parameters and causal boundaries, with relevant calculations adapted for extremal black holes and associated supersymmetric solutions.

Recent advancements in Deep Learning have enabled the creation of highly effective end-to-end learning systems for complex tasks like engine control system design. Research has shown that incorporating theoretical knowledge into deep learning models can lead to significant performance improvements. A new study aims to optimize end-to-end learning for automatic engine speed regulation using a dynamic system model and a novel loss function. This approach was evaluated using data from an experimental engine and was found to outperform a standard comparison method. Additionally, the results demonstrate that end-to-end learning can be more efficient than traditional model predictive control methods.

A generalized version of the Poincaré group, accounting for special and general relativity, along with the principles of quantum mechanics, is the basis for the theoretical framework being developed. The traditional approach of quantizing a particle in flat space is reversed, with the particle's momentum generating a commutator that defines a non-trivial, curved space. The associated curvature, expressed as the momentum tensor, is recognized as the fundamental force driving physics. The strategies for the particle mechanisms, where the curvature peaks, indicating mass generation, are being explored.

Designing parameterized algorithms for specific graph problems has become increasingly important. Specifically, this study focuses on upward planarity – a graph layout where nodes are arranged in a hierarchical, upward manner. We've developed parameterized approaches to upward planarity that rely on specific graph properties. First, we've created a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of face indentations to identify whether a given graph can be laid out in an upward planar format. We've also developed a parameterized problem for detecting whether a directed path exists in an acyclic graph, which is influenced by the number of backward edges. Furthermore, we've established a parameterized trichotomy for outerplanar graphs, as well as developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on treewidth to lay out these graphs in an upward planar format. We've also derived a fixed-parameter algorithm based on treedepth for this same problem. We introduce new sufficient and necessary conditions for outerplanar graphs to be laid out in an upward planar format. We show that these conditions allow us to efficiently generate a linear layout for these graphs. We've developed a new parameterized approach to detecting whether a given directed acyclic graph can be laid out in an upward planar format, which is based on the number of source nodes in the graph. We've established a new parameterized approach to detecting whether a given outerplanar graph can be laid out in an upward planar format, which is based on the number of vertices in the graph

Memories of past navigation experiences in virtual environments are recalled as visual representations. However, not all recollections are equally relevant to current situations. This research introduces MemoNav, a system that identifies and prioritizes the most helpful navigation history based on the principles of insensitivity to irrelevant details and global perspective. By leveraging the Tree Transformer architecture, MemoNav learns to connect navigation memories through common features, effectively integrating multiple memories to guide future interactions. Our experiments with various methods in diverse tasks, such as searching for hidden targets in real-world environments or robing shops in video game-style scenarios, consistently demonstrate MemoNav's superiority over other approaches.

In sixth-generation (6G) wireless technology, compact cells play a crucial role in addressing impending communication issues. To gain insight into the future of 6G compact cells, we need to examine their development from 6G to 4G. Therefore, we've categorized indoor wireless networks into 6G, 5G, and 4G in this paper, and we're investigating the underlying trends, the challenges we've faced, and the prospects we're likely to encounter. It's worth noting that the size and coverage of compact cells are key factors, and their impact is being felt from reconfigurable 6G millimeter-wave to hand-thin 4G wearable devices. We've explored the historical and modern aspects of compact cells, including their design, the spectrum available to them, and deployment methods. Furthermore, we've discussed the prospects and challenges compact cells may encounter in the future.

A new concept, called a hypergraph dynamical network, is introduced by combining a physical network and a biological network within a specified time frame. The proposed model aims to simulate networks composed of complex relationships between individual entities through interactive processes over time. Additionally, a measure of dynamic network centrality is developed to quantify the importance of network components by tracking their activity levels throughout various time periods. Using this centrality measure, research findings on brain networks and other systems are expected to provide insights into their functioning and inform diagnosis and treatment decisions.

We examine how the operator product expansion (OPE) relates to the solution of the Yang-Baxter equation in 2D quantum field theories. By applying the OPE in a specific region and then shifting the location of one of the operators, we investigate the connection between the resulting expressions. This analysis leads us to utilize the coefficients of the OPE, which we refer to as kernels, to decompose the state space of primary fields and identify a key component, the twist field. Furthermore, our study reveals a crucial property of twist fields, which serves as the basis for a novel proof of conformal symmetry in 2D models. Additionally, our research explores the behavior of twist fields in various fractal growth models and identifies a distinctive pattern.

The Heisenberg's Many Body Project's theoretical calculation for the Hoyle state's direct decay component, which considers a $0.98$ fraction of decay, is largely in line with experimental evidence. Although recent studies at Jefferson Lab have provided support for this theoretical framework, a significant issue remains regarding the reliance on unbounded nuclear wave functions near the boundaries. To address this limitation, we propose utilizing a new, nearly medium-free method for calculating the Hoyle state's direct decay component, which relies on the response function's integral computation within a large finite nuclear volume. By applying this concept to a theoretical model with a large but finite nuclear volume, we demonstrate that the Hoyle state's $0s1$ state decay ratio can be accurately determined. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the analytical formulas for the nuclear response functions enable the calculation of the Hoyle state's direct and indirect decay components without reliance on bound nuclear wave functions near the boundaries, thus significantly simplifying the computation.

Significant advances have been made in understanding the dynamics of cracking in brittle materials. Research has made headway despite the intricacy of the problem, albeit with unresolved aspects. The length and time scales inherent to such materials still mystery to scientists. This study uses advanced simulations to explore the roles of these scales in shaping the behavior of cracks. The researchers found that their model accurately replicated renowned experiments, including the study of crack branching. They explored the effects of material properties on crack behavior, varying only one factor to isolate its impact. The results showed that changes in one property led to a shift from oscillating to "tip-dividing" branching. Further analysis revealed that this shift was linked to a critical balance between inherent material lengths and times. This finding has important implications for modeling and can inform future experiments.

We have examined two distinct communication systems that rely on the sender having complete knowledge of the receiver's encoding method. In the first scenario, the receiver has access to real-time feedback about the sent messages, while only limited information about the underlying system is available. Our objective is to identify optimal strategies for both the sender and receiver that result in minimal errors, while also exploring the extent to which feedback can be replicated through proactive actions taken by the receiver. In the second context, the receiver seeks to gain as much as possible about the underlying system without knowing its properties, while also utilizing real-time feedback from the sent messages. Our goal is to find the best possible ways for both parties to act in order to minimize errors in the latter scenario. 

We have found that in the first context, the sender only needs to use fixed codes to respond to the receiver's actions, while using variable length codes to process the received feedback. Additionally, we have found that in the second context, the receiver has an optimal approach to balancing exploration and exploitation of the underlying system's properties, particularly when using real-time feedback. 

Our study is based on two key studies, one by Bergman and Csiszar, and another by Bergman. We have also made connections to two distinct research areas - one related to control theory and another to information theory. 

Our approach to tackling these problems is to utilize tools from functional analysis, while our results in both contexts turn out to be equivalent to results from two distinct research areas

Quantum systems exhibiting both Rashba spin-orbit coupling and interparticle attraction may form complex superpositions of fermions. In a recent study, researchers utilized a mean-field approach and Gaudin model to analyze the phase structure of an attractive Rashba Hubbard chain with a finite number of bosonic particles. Their calculations showed that particle-particle interaction Rabi-like oscillations and spin-decoupling occur on the superfluidity timescale. Utilizing a spin-symmetric phase approximation, the researchers identified a wide range of parameters where a spin-singlet superfluid phase emerges. Furthermore, the calculations demonstrated that spin-singlet paired bosons migrate towards the Fermi sea as a result of an effective attractive potential. Our findings also reveal that spin-depopulation is a inherent consequence of superfluidity and spin-singlet pairing. Our analytical framework offers a versatile tool to investigate topological superfluidity in systems featuring Rashba spin-orbit coupling and particle-particle attraction.

This study focuses on fact validation and proof discovery within tabular data found in scientific publications. To address this challenge, we introduce a new dataset comprising 1,000 tables selected from over 5,000 in the PubMed database. This dataset includes 1,000 verified facts, 1,000 invalid facts, and 1,000 tables containing multiple relationships. We outline a two-stage task: first, fact validation, and second, identifying supporting proofs within these tables. In the companion paper, we provide comprehensive guidelines for the proposed task, its rationale, and the proposed dataset. We invite participants to engage in this challenge through a competition hosted at the SemEval 2021 conference.

This note explores the connection between intricate numbers and quantum physics, specifically examining the complex representation of phases in Schrödinger's equation and the Pauli matrices within Dirac's equations. We examine complex numbers in the context of these equations, noting their distinct roles in contrast to intricate numbers, which could potentially replace complex numbers in these equations. However, due to differences in equations such as the Schrödinger equation and the Dirac equation, intricate numbers are not necessarily applicable. Nevertheless, in quantum mechanics based on Pauli matrices, we identify potential applications of intricate numbers, particularly in connection with Geometric Algebra and the Argand plane.

The metric dimension of a graph is defined as the minimum number of vertices that can pinpoint every other vertex using shortest path distances. A subspace of this concept, called semi-metric dimension, focuses on identifying vertices that can locate every other vertex within a specific shortest path distance threshold. Two notable parameters in this area are the semi-metric dimension and effective diameter, which, for certain graphs, can be linked to the minimum number of spanning trees. Our research introduces two metrics: the weak semi-metric dimension and the strong semi-metric dimension. The weak semi-metric dimension represents the minimum number of vertices that can identify every other vertex using at least one shortest path distance measurement, whereas the strong semi-metric dimension represents the minimum number of vertices that can pinpoint every other vertex using specific shortest path distance measurements in all cases. Our main findings compare these parameters to the metric dimension and effective diameter of various graphs, including paths, cycles, cubes, and complete graphs. Additionally, we analyzed how these parameters change when changing specific edge weights in these graphs. Furthermore, we investigated how our strong semi-metric dimension approach applies to locating problems in graphs.

Calculating the cost of injecting pressurized fluids into the ground is a complex task that requires considering various factors such as stress waves, permeability, and pressurization levels. To address this issue, two formulations have been developed for modeling fluid injection into homogeneous and heterogeneous soils. The first approach utilizes a simplified method for stress wave propagation, while the second formulation incorporates more detailed equations. Additionally, an analysis of stress wave energy was presented to facilitate the comparison of these formulations.

This study proposes an innovative method to effectively remove sulfur dioxide from flue gas using ozone generated from ultraviolet light.  By combining UV light and ozone, the reaction time required to achieve the same level of removal is significantly reduced from 2.5 seconds to just 0.15 seconds.  Notably, the energy needed to accomplish this is comparable to current methods, once ozone is produced.  To optimize this process, we investigated various parameters using response surface methodology.  The results of our experiments revealed that removal efficiency is optimal when the ozone concentration is around 30-40 milligrams per liter, temperature ranges from 30 to 50 degrees Celsius, and the UV dose is between 1600 and 2000 mu J/cm^2.  Using these conditions, the removal rate of sulfur dioxide reached 98% along with the reduction of nitrogen oxides, which is crucial considering the harmful effects of nitrogen oxides on the environment.

As interest in neuromorphic computing continues to grow, engineers face significant challenges in designing and simulating this innovative hardware. While SystemC is a popular choice for simulating complex digital systems, implementing neuromorphic architectures within SystemC can be a complex task. Researchers have created various virtual platforms to facilitate simulation, but these often lack key features required for realistic modeling. Moreover, most available platforms are tailored to specific architecture designs, limiting their applicability to others. In response to these challenges, we have developed a new framework, SCNMP, to simplify the creation and simulation of neuromorphic architectures within SystemC. This modular framework provides a set of reusable components to model neural networks, allowing for easy adaptation to different architecture designs via customisation of its component sub-classes. SCNMP features a range of advanced simulation capabilities, including event-driven and time-driven execution modes, as well as support for tau-based networks. To validate its effectiveness, we have used SCNMP to simulate two distinct neuromorphic architectures: a RAM-based synaptic array and a finite-state machine-based neural network. With its flexible design, SCNMP can be used to simulate a broad spectrum of neuromorphic architectures, making it an invaluable tool for architects, simulator developers, and researchers in the field of neuromorphic computing.

Machine learning models can learn to classify data using pre-defined categories, but they can't address uncertainties inherent in data, which can lead to misclassification. In contrast, expert systems can incorporate nuanced reasoning about such uncertainties, often framed as arguments with associated weights. Expert systems can represent this uncertainty through sets of possible interpretations, known as semantics-alternative logic. In this context, we propose a new learning paradigm, Indecision Forests, which can acquire decision-making rules based on data, taking into account both categories and arguments, as well as their associated uncertainties. In this study, we demonstrate how Indecision Forests can be realized using a relational machine learning framework, and we explore its potential advantages and limitations.

The pruned dynamic time warping (PruneDTW) algorithm is an efficient method for guiding the search in dynamic time warning distances. By eliminating unsuitable candidate matches, it speeds up the execution time. A key component of PruneDTW is the decision threshold, which determines the candidate matches to discard. Choosing the optimal threshold value is crucial, as it may lead to suboptimal results if not ideal. We introduce an enhanced version of PruneDTW, early discarding pruned dynamic time warping (EDPruneDTW), that involves determining the optimal threshold value automatically. In addition, we examine the potential applications of PruneDTW and its variants in similarity search tasks. Our analysis demonstrates that EDPruneDTW yields comparable results to PruneDTW, yet offers improved performance in certain scenarios.

In educational settings, providing effective feedback in introductory computing courses can be challenging, particularly when dealing with large student populations. This study compares traditional detailed feedback methods with a newer approach, inquiry-based conceptual feedback, in the context of introductory computing courses focused on software testing. Through an online survey, we gathered responses from 174 students, examining their preferences for each method.
